articles.title: Chris Rock Says Infidelity and Struggling to ‘Make It’ Aren’t Just Hollywood Problems: ‘If You Got No Love, You’re Broke as F—k’
articles.summary: Chris Rock’s new movie “Misty Green” centers on a fictional actress (Rosalind Eleazar) mounting a Hollywood comeback after years in the throes of a fading career. Misty’s journey pokes fun at some of the trappings of trying to “make it” in the entertainment industry, a pursuit that Rock himself is…
body: “I don’t think it’s a Hollywood thing, it’s just life,” Rock told Variety. “Our two characters bond over our infidelities. And, yeah, it’s a lot. But it’s show business, man. Rock ’n’ roll!”

“Misty Green” also marks a real-life underdog moment for Eleazar, who tops the call sheet on a feature film for the first time. Following its premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival, Variety chief awards editor Clayton Davis declared that Eleazar “is a best actress contender that dares anyone in the room to argue otherwise.”

“I’ve had bouts of not working,” Eleazar explained. “ I know many actors that have had huge bouts of not working and are constantly knocked down. And I have a lot of respect for actors that get up and do it all over again. But it’s also a universal story about any industry. It’s not just about actors.”

Rounding out the ensemble are Adam Driver, Daniel Kaluuya, Anna Kendrick and Topher Grace. On just a $5 million price tag, Rock says he was able to assemble a star-studded cast for “Misty Green” by keeping the production local to Los Angeles.

articles.title: ‘A joyful place’: a new museum coaxes Austrians to embrace The Sound of Music
articles.summary: Sixty years after the film’s release, Salzburg is embracing a Hollywood classic it once kept at arm’s length. Let’s start at the very beginning – famously, a very good place to start.
body: Just two decades after the second world war, a Hollywood crew descended on Salzburg with stars, show tunes and a compelling, essentially true story of love and opposition to Adolf Hitler: The Sound of Music.
The Austrian city, still economically and morally devastated from the Nazi period, wasn’t quite ready to receive them.

Although director Robert Wise was free to make use of the glorious Alpine settings and the old town’s historical facades, scenes such as soldiers marching across the central Residenzplatz under swastika flags made municipal authorities deeply uneasy.
When the film premiered in 1965, it ran for a couple of weeks, closed for lack of ticket sales and largely disappeared from local memory. That is until the tour buses started coming.

articles.title: Roger Ebert Gave A Perfect Score To This Woody Harrelson Crime Thriller No One Talks About
articles.summary: The great Roger Ebert once gave a perfect rating to a 2012 crime thriller starring Woody Harrelson that no one really talks about these days.
body: In 2012, Woody Harrelson starred in "Rampart," a crime drama that, though well-reviewed, was a box office bomb. Still, a perfect review from Roger Ebert surely helped partially make up for the film's commercial performance, with the esteemed critic heaping praise on this gritty tale of a corrupt LAPD veteran who's forced to reckon with his shady legacy.

One man who certainly wouldn't have forgotten the movie, however, is Ebert. The critic, who passed away at the age of 70 in 2013, gave "Rampart" a full four stars, praising Harrelson for his performance as a morally bankrupt crooked cop backed into a corner. While not everybody found it to be one of the greatest thrillers of the 21st century, it should at least be remembered more widely than it is, and, according to Ebert, might even deserve a spot on that list.

articles.title: Naomi Watts Praises Husband Billy Crudup for Backing Her Menopause Activism: “So Sweet — and Sexy”
articles.summary: Zurich's Golden Eye recipient also charted her 10 years of unsuccessful auditions before getting her big break in 'Mulholland Drive': "My agent told me, 'Honey, you're too intense. You're freaking people out.'"
body: It felt like Naomi Watts covered it all in a Zurich Film Festival masterclass on Sunday afternoon: dreams, drama and, of course, the menopause.

The British star opened up with host Max Loong about struggling for around a decade auditioning in Los Angeles before she would go on to meet David Lynch and star in his career-transforming Mulholland Drive. Watts was speaking the day after a glitzy Zurich ceremony in which she accepted the fest’s prestigious Golden Eye award for her latest feature, The Housewife.

In a bizarre way, meeting the late, great Lynch — whom Watts did an impeccable impression of, pretend cigarette and all — was almost like therapy for the actress, who landed that breakout role at the age of 31. She was worn down by Hollywood’s faux interest in her talent and the fickle nature with which casting directors operated. “[You’d] line up and see 10 or 15 girls, running their lines, looking much better for the part than you do, and it was really a grind,” Watts told the room.

articles.title: 5 Forgotten Pirate Movies That Still Hold Up Today
articles.summary: Avast! Here be five forgotten pirate movies that still hold up in 2026, involving everything from space pirates to scallywags who sail the seven seas.
body: It's been a good 18 to 20 years since the internet was properly obsessed with pirates. I merrily recall the "pirates vs. ninjas" debate with clarity, with the two professions eternally locked in a dead heat. What was more appealing: Plundering, looting, drinking rum, and living on the high seas? Or living in the shadows of Japan, mastering hundreds of awesome oblique weapons and killing people for a tidy payment?

When it came to cinematic evidence to argue both points, however, pirates always had the advantage. Pirate movies are practically as old as the medium, with some pirate classics stretching back to the 1920s and 1930s. Ninjas didn't become a proper cinematic fixture until unleashed by certain Cannon Group movies in the early 1980s. Of course, a certain generation grew up watching those ninja movies, so the profession was just as deeply entrenched in their subconsciousness. The argument essentially boils down to youth vs. experience. Of course, given that pirate movies and TV shows are still being made and ninja films seem dated, pirates have, overall, won the internet's debate.

articles.title: Israeli Americans Protest Outside ‘NAZA’ New York Premiere by Screening Oct. 7 Attacks Footage
articles.summary: Israeli-American Council (IAC) co-chair Tal Shuster said of the Israel–Gaza war documentary, "We're not saying, don't show the film. We're saying: show all the facts."
body: Dozens of Israeli Americans and members of Jewish communities gathered outside the Lincoln Center on Saturday to protest the premiere of NAZA at the New York Film Festival.

The documentary, directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, was filmed at night from Tel Aviv rooftops and examines “the systems behind the mass killing of Palestinian civilians” by Israel ‘s military operations in Gaza, the filmmakers previously said.

“We’re here not because we’re saying, don’t show the film,” Israeli-American Council (IAC) co-chair Tal Shuster said of NAZA during the rally. “Everyone has the freedom of speech, that’s the United States. We are saying: it’s not all the facts. Show everything else, not just the documentary.”

“We have the trucks here,” Shuster continued. “Let’s each one of us be an ambassador and show people what actually happened. If you screen the film, invite a survivor, let them speak, at a panel. Let them be heard. Don’t just show one side without the facts from the other side. Before you go into the film, or after it, come hear about what happened in Israel on Oct. 7. 1,200 people were murdered. 251 people were kidnapped. Yes, show all the facts.”

articles.title: NAZA film-makers address threats at documentary’s New York City premiere
articles.summary: Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor defend findings on Israel’s killing of Palestinians amid threats from Israeli officials. The film-makers behind NAZA, the award-winning documentary on Israel’s systemic mass killing of Palestinians in Gaza, defended their findings at the film’s North American premiere…
body: The critically acclaimed film, directed by Oscar-winning film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and produced by the Guardian, features the testimony of 24 anonymized Israeli soldiers and intelligence officers involved in the surveillance and remote killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza, who describe the AI-powered systems used to select their targets. The project takes its name from an acronym used euphemistically by Israeli intelligence to indicate how many civilians it expects to die in an airstrike, which are often conducted at night in private homes, killing many family members, including children, at once.

“Our country is doing so much to hide these systems,” Szor told the audience at the New York film festival in a Q&A that followed the film’s premiere. “It’s not a world that is open even to the Israeli public.”
“These crimes that you saw are ongoing,” Abraham said. “They’re ongoing because it’s what our country is doing, and because of what your country is supporting and funding.”
